summary.text:
Every pound Swale owes matures inside two years, and 82% of it inside twelve months. There is exactly one PWLB loan — £3m drawn on 26 March 2026 at 4.92% — and everything else is money borrowed from six other district and borough councils. One of those, £2.1m from Maidstone at 6.25%, ran from 19 March to 1 April: thirteen days at over six per cent.

The number that stands out is the pair either side of it. The book costs 4.88%. The investment portfolio returned 3.61% — below their own 4.19% estimate, below average Bank Rate of 4.04% and below SONIA at 4.01% — on £23m of average daily balances. They were borrowing at 4.88% and investing at 3.61% at the same time.

The balance sheet reconciles exactly: CFR £62.267m less £17.100m of borrowing is the £45.167m cumulative external borrowing requirement they state, and the liability benchmark rebuilds to £16.6m to the pound. The CCLA holding is carried at £2.8m against £3.0m of cost, which is what the £350k statutory override reserve is for.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual treasury report that went to Audit Committee on 15 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. You hold one PWLB loan and we hold the same one — £3,000,000 at 4.92% maturing 27 September 2027, drawn in the last week of March. Your paragraph 2.8 table sums to £17.100m, and CFR of £62.267m less that leaves the £45.167m cumulative external borrowing requirement you show at 2.1. Your liability benchmark rebuilds the same way: £62.3m less £55.7m of balance sheet resources is £6.6m, plus the £10.0m liquidity allowance gives £16.6m. All of it ties.

The thing we would put in front of you is two numbers from different pages of your own report. The borrowing book costs 4.88%. The investment portfolio returned 3.61% — against your own 4.19% estimate, against average Bank Rate of 4.04%, and against average SONIA of 4.01%. On £23m of average daily balances, you were borrowing at 4.88% and investing at 3.61% through the same year.

We have no recommendation about that and it is not our place to have one — the borrowing is funding capital and the investments are working balances, so they are not directly substitutable, and you will know the cashflow reasons far better than we can from a report. What we would say is that the gap is the kind of thing that is easier to see against the rest of the sector than on its own. Money market funds paying 3.93% is roughly where the market was; the question is what the £23m of average balances was doing relative to what it cost to carry.

The second thing is the shape. 82% of your debt matures inside twelve months and 100% inside two years. There is no long-dated debt at all. Six of the seven loans are from other district and borough councils — Spelthorne, Ashfield twice, Amber Valley, Tamworth and Maidstone — and the Maidstone one, £2.1m at 6.25%, ran from 19 March to 1 April. Thirteen days at over six per cent tells you exactly what the year-end market looked like, and your own paragraph 2.6 says the same thing: local authority rates "between 4.0% and 4.5%" for most of the year, then "5.0% - 7.0%" towards the year end.

That is precisely the market nobody publishes. Every council sees its own trades and none sees the distribution, so there is no way from inside one treasury to know whether 6.25% for a fortnight was the going rate that week or the top of it. We track inter-authority pricing across the sector alongside the PWLB side, and July's PWLB lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — thin, which is when short-dated inter-authority money gets expensive. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

For what it is worth on the other side: one-year PWLB certainty closed at 4.95% this afternoon on notice 314/26, two-year at 5.06% and five-year at 5.34%. Your single PWLB loan is currently about £29,000 in premium on the DMO's premature repayment curve, which is to say essentially at par — nothing to do there and we are not suggesting otherwise. We don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote.

One small note. Your 10-year certainty range for the year — 5.38% at the start, 5.72% at the end, 5.13% low and 5.88% high — is identical to what three other Arlingclose clients have reported to us this summer, and it matches our own series. When we say something about the market we are speaking the same language as your adviser.

On training, four fit Swale. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets is the obvious one given six of seven loans. Liquidity & cashflow forecasting for the borrowing-versus-investing question. Pooled funds (CCLA, multi-asset), given the £2.8m fair value against £3.0m of cost and the £350k override reserve you have decided to keep. And Liability Benchmark: using it in practice — yours forecasts down to £11.5m by 2028, which is a genuinely useful thing to be able to show members. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
